newsitem.title: USA: Clinton warns Palestinians against violence.
newsitem.headline: Clinton warns Palestinians against violence.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Monday said he regretted Israel's plan to build Jewish housing in Arab East Jerusalem but warned the Palestinians it would be a "terrible mistake" to resort to violence over the matter.

Speaking at a news conference with Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak, Clinton said recent events showed how difficult it is to make progress toward peace in the Middle East and called on all parties in the region to redouble their efforts.

Israeli-Palestinian negotiations have been roiled in recent weeks by several events, including an Israeli decision to build 6,500 housing units in a part of Arab East Jerusalem and its taking steps to close four PLO offices in the city.

In addition, the top Palestinian negotiator resigned on Monday after Israel's decision to hand back nine percent of the territory it occupies in the West Bank, rather than the 30 percent the Palestinians had expected.

At least 10 Palestinians were injured in clashes on Monday with Israeli soldiers when 150 soldiers used clubs and guns to beat back 100 Palestinians trying to stop workers from opening a road for Jewish settlers near the West Bank city of Hebron.

"We've also been reminded recently of how difficult it is to maintain the momentum toward peace," Clinton said. "Clearly we're at a moment when all those with a stake in the peace process must rededicate themselves to ... making progress."

"We made it very clear that the decision to build (Jewish housing in East Jerusalem) ... would not build confidence, would not be conducive to negotiations. We would prefer strongly that it not have been made."
He added: "I still believe it would be a terrible mistake for the Palestinians to resort to violence. Every time they have done it, they wind up losing. They wind up getting hurt."
The U.S. president also defended the U.S. decision to veto a U.N. resolution urging Israel to abandon the housing plan.

Clinton applied the same reasoning to the U.S. stance on both issues, saying the Jerusalem housing and the U.N. motion touched on "final status" issues that are to be hammered out in direct talks between Israel and the Palestinians.
Those talks are due to begin on March 17.
"The best thing is ... to let them be resolved by negotiations and to decide final status issues without interference by anyone from the outside," Clinton said.

But Mubarak politely disagreed on the issue of vetoing the U.N. resolution issue, saying: "It is unfortunate that the resolution was not adopted because it may have given a signal to the Israelis to stop any settlement activies, especially in the area of Jerusalem, which is illegal.
"But I hope in the future we could avoid this," he said.

The Egyptian leader had warm words for Clinton as a partner in the peacemaking process, nonetheless, but he said he was "alarmed" by Israeli actions -- including the housing decision -- which he said tended to undermine peace efforts.
Clinton said he and Mubarak, who talked for about three hours on Monday, had agreed to seek ways to try to revive the Syrian-Israeli track of the Middle East peace process.

Their meeting was one of a series between Clinton and the main regional players as Washington assesses how to proceed towards a comprehensive peace settlement despite a backdrop of continuing Israeli-Palestinian strife.

Mubarak is the third Middle Eastern leader to visit the White House in the past month, following Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's visit on February 13 and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's visit last week.
Jordan's King Hussein is due here for talks next Tuesday.
Earlier on Monday, Arafat said Israel's decision on the West Bank pullout, the first phase of which was expected to go forward this week, had violated Netanyahu's peace promises.
"There is a real crisis because there is a clear breaching to what had been agreed upon," Arafat saidin Gaza, calling the move "a trick and a conspiracy against the peace process."
